title: Web Linking
summary: This specification defines a model for how web resources relate to each other, called links, and for the type of each relationship, called link relation types. It also defines how to put links in HTTP headers using the Link header field.

eli5.summary: Web pages can say, here is the next page or here is the author. This defines a standard way to put those pointers in the message headers.

questions: what is the http link header
how does the link header anchor parameter work
how do i register a link relation type
subtitle: A standard way to say how one web resource relates to another, and to carry those links in an HTTP Link header.

tldr.problem: HTML and Atom each had their own idea of a link, and there was no common model for how resources relate or a way to convey links in HTTP headers.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8288 defines a link as a context, a relation type, a target and optional target attributes, and defines the Link header field to serialise one or more links in HTTP.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 5988 and keeps the model and the Link header field, with clarified cardinality, explicit whitespace in the ABNF and a suggested parsing algorithm.

today: RFC 8288 is a Proposed Standard and obsoletes RFC 5988. The metadata for this unit lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Link Model
sections.content:
RFC 8288 defines a model for the relationships between resources on the Web, called links, and for the type of those relationships, called link relation types. HTML and Atom already had well-defined linking, and the RFC generalises them into a framework that can cover those formats and potentially others.

It also defines the Link HTTP header field, which carries such links in HTTP headers. The RFC obsoletes RFC 5988.
sections.eli5: A link is like a signpost that says which way to go and what you will find there. This document says how to write signposts so every program reads them the same way.

sections.title: The Link Model
sections.content:
A link is a typed connection between two resources. It has a link context, a link relation type, a link target and, optionally, target attributes. It reads as a statement: the context has a resource of the relation type at the target, which has the target attributes. The RFC's example is that https://www.example.com/ has a canonical resource at https://example.com, which has a type of text/html.

Contexts and targets are Internationalized Resource Identifiers (IRIs), though in the common case the context is also a URI. There are no restrictions on cardinality: there can be many links to and from a target, and several links of the same or different types between one context and target. The order of links is not specified or significant.

Links travel in link serialisations (the bytes on the wire) and are used by link applications. The RFC does not define a general syntax across serialisations, and does not mandate a context for any given link. For example, the application "Web browsing" looks for the stylesheet relation type in HTML, while AtomPub uses edit and edit-media in Atom.
sections.eli5: A link is a sentence: this page has a cover picture over there. It has a who, a what kind of relationship, and a where.

sections.title: Link Relation Types
sections.content:
A link relation type identifies the meaning of a link, for example copyright means the context has a copyright resource at the target. Relation types are not media types: they do not describe the format you get when you follow the link, only how the context relates to the target. They SHOULD NOT infer extra meaning from the presence or absence of another relation type, with one historical exception: alternate combined with stylesheet has special meaning in HTML.

There are two kinds. Registered types are tokens listed in the IANA Link Relations registry. Their names MUST be compared character by character, case-insensitively, and they MUST NOT constrain the media type of the context or target. Registration uses the Specification Required policy: a request gives a name, a short description and a reference, and it must point to a freely available, stable specification. The designated expert is told to be strongly biased towards approval unless a request is abusive, frivolous, unlikely to be used on the Internet or actively harmful.

Extension types are URIs that uniquely identify the relation. Clients SHOULD NOT automatically fetch that URI, to avoid overburdening its server. Extension types are compared as strings, case-insensitively, so all-lowercase URIs SHOULD be used. Turning a registered name into a URI by adding a base is NOT RECOMMENDED, because other applications will not treat the result as equivalent.
sections.eli5: A relation type is the label on the signpost, like "next" or "author". Common labels go on an official list, and if you need a special one you can use your own web address as its name.

sections.title: The Link Header Field
sections.content:
The Link header field serialises one or more links. Each link-value is a URI-Reference in angle brackets followed by any number of semicolon-separated parameters. The ABNF is Link = #link-value, link-value = "<" URI-Reference ">" *( OWS ";" OWS link-param ) and link-param = token BWS [ "=" BWS ( token / quoted-string ) ].

Recipients MUST accept both forms of a parameter value, so x=y and x="y" are equivalent. Senders wanting maximum interoperability keep the older habits: title quoted and hreflang as a token.

The link target is the URI-Reference in the angle brackets. A relative reference MUST be resolved as in RFC 3986, and any base IRI in the message content is not applied. The link context defaults to the URL of the representation the header comes with. The anchor parameter overrides it, for example with a fragment of this resource or a third resource. An application may ignore links with an anchor, but then it MUST ignore the whole link rather than process it without the anchor. On some responses, such as a 404 to a GET, the context is anonymous.
sections.eli5: The Link header is a list on the envelope. Each entry gives an address in angle brackets and then a few labels after semicolons, like "this is the previous chapter".

sections.title: Relation and Target Parameters
sections.content:
The relation type goes in the rel parameter. It MUST be present and MUST NOT appear more than once; occurrences after the first MUST be ignored. It can hold several space-separated relation types, which establishes several links sharing the same context, target and target attributes. Registered names are lowercase letters, digits, dots and hyphens. Extension types in a Link header MUST be absolute URIs, and MUST be quoted if they contain characters such as a semicolon or comma. The rev parameter, which expressed the reverse relationship, is deprecated because it confuses authors and readers.

Five parameters are defined as target attributes for this serialisation:

  • hreflang: a hint about the language of the target. Several can appear to say several languages are available.
  • media: the intended medium for style information. It MUST NOT appear more than once and MUST be quoted if it contains a semicolon or comma.
  • title: a human-readable label such as a menu entry. It MUST NOT appear more than once.
  • title*: the same label encoded per RFC 8187, allowing another character set and language. If both appear, applications SHOULD use the starred value.
  • type: a hint about the target's media type. It MUST NOT appear more than once.

The hreflang and type values are only hints and do not override the Content-Language or Content-Type of the actual response. Other parameters are extension attributes. A parameter name ending in an asterisk may use the RFC 8187 encoding, and applications SHOULD prefer its decoded value.
sections.eli5: The rel label says what kind of signpost it is, and it may only be given once. Extra labels like title or language are helpful hints, not promises.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives these Link header examples:

  • Link: <http://example.com/TheBook/chapter2>; rel="previous"; title="previous chapter" says chapter2 is previous to this resource in a logical navigation path.
  • Link: </terms>; rel="copyright"; anchor="#foo" says the copyright terms apply only to the part of the document identified by the fragment foo.
  • A single header can carry several links, with title*=UTF-8'de'letztes%20Kapitel showing non-ASCII text and the German language tag de.
  • rel="start http://example.net/relation/other" gives one target both a registered type, start, and an extension type.

A header with two comma-separated link-values is equivalent to sending the same two links in two separate Link header fields.
sections.eli5: These examples show real-looking signposts: previous chapter, copyright terms for just one part, and a chapter title written in German.

sections.title: Security and Internationalisation
sections.content:
The content of a Link header field is not secure, private or integrity-guaranteed. Using TLS with HTTP is, per the RFC, currently the only end-to-end way to provide those properties.

Link applications should think about the risks of automatically following, trusting or using links from headers. Links with an anchor are effectively assertions by a third party that could be wrong or malicious, so an application can discard them unless a relationship between the resources, such as the same authority, is established. Dereferencing links has its own risks: the Referer header can expose private application state, and cookies can become an attack vector.

On internationalisation, link targets and the anchor value may need conversion from IRIs to URIs because the Link header cannot carry IRIs. Relation types are URIs, not IRIs, to aid comparison, and registered names are lowercase ASCII letters.
sections.eli5: A signpost on an envelope could be a trick. Do not walk down a path just because a stranger's sign says to, and do not tell the place you arrive at where you came from if that is private.

sections.title: Parsing Guidance and Changes from RFC 5988
sections.content:
Appendix B gives non-normative parsing algorithms for the Link header: parsing a header set, a field value, the parameters and a quoted string. They are more permissive than the ABNF and advisory only; the body of the specification governs if they disagree.

Appendix A notes how HTML link elements and Atom atom:link elements map onto the model. In Atom, link relation types are compared case-sensitively and a single link-value may map to several atom:link elements.

Appendix C lists changes from RFC 5988, among them: the initial relation type registrations and the Link Relation Application Data registry were removed, link cardinality and the cardinality of target attributes were clarified, terminology moved from "target IRI" and "context IRI" to "link target" and "link context", the default link context was corrected to depend on the representation, and the ABNF was updated to be compatible with RFC 7230 with whitespace now explicit.
